notes.title: -다고 하다
notes.text: To report what someone said, add -다고 하다: 비가 온다고 했어요 (they said it'll rain), 맛있다고 해요 (people say it's tasty), 학생이라고 했어요 (she said she's a student). Korea's provinces end in 도 (강원도, 경기도…), and each has its own dialect — 경상도 사투리 is a favorite in dramas.

notes.title: -냐고 묻다
notes.text: To report a question, use -냐고 묻다 or -냐고 하다: 어디 가냐고 물었어요 (She asked where I was going). 해외 = overseas, 국내 = domestic. Foreign city names are borrowed sounds: 뉴욕, 런던, 파리, 도쿄 (older name 동경), 베이징 (older name 북경).

notes.title: Getting around Korea
notes.text: The KTX bullet train links Seoul with most big cities in two or three hours. 고속버스 (express buses) leave from big terminals and are cheap and comfy. 시외버스 serve smaller towns. Seoul has two airports: 인천공항 (international) and 김포공항 (mostly domestic).

notes.title: Places to stay
notes.text: 호텔 (hotel), 여관 (old-style inn, simple and cheap), 민박 (a room in a local home), 펜션 (a countryside cottage, great for groups), 게스트하우스 (guesthouse). In farming villages you can try 농촌 체험 — a day of farm life. 군 after a young man's name (민준 군) is an old-fashioned, affectionate "young Mr."

notes.title: Seoul sights
notes.text: 경복궁 and 덕수궁 are royal palaces; 남산 (with N Seoul Tower) has the best view of the city; 종로 is the historic downtown; 동대문시장 is a giant market that stays open late into the night. Before a trip, Koreans ask 짐 쌌어? (Did you pack?) and 준비물 챙겼어?
